\section{Multicolour extension and numerical experiments}

\subsection{A multicolour extension of size-biased survival}
\label{qua:app:multicolour}

The size-biased mechanism is not specific to two colours.  Suppose every edge
has one of $q\ge2$ colours, and let
\[
 r=q(K-2)+1,
 \qquad
 B_d=1+q+\cdots+q^{d-1}=\frac{q^d-1}{q-1}.
\]
Choose the power of two
\[
 L_q=2^{\lceil\log_2(2B_r)\rceil},
\]
so $2B_r\le L_q<4B_r$.  If the $s-1$ non-pivot vertices split into sizes
$a_1,\ldots,a_q$, the induction in \cref{qua:lem:size-biased-survival} becomes
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^q (a_j-B_{d-1})_+
 \ge
 \left(s-1-qB_{d-1}\right)_+
 =(s-B_d)_+,
\]
because $B_d=1+qB_{d-1}$.  Thus, for $d\ge1$, the $d$-step survival
probability is at least $(s-B_d)_+/(s-1)$ when $s\ge2$.  Starting from
$L_q\ge2B_r$ gives probability greater than $1/2$, and among the $r$
recorded colours one occurs at least $K-1$ times.

\begin{corollary}[Multicolour size-biased Ramsey search]
\label{qua:cor:multicolour}
For $q,K\ge2$, every $q$-edge-coloured complete graph on at least $L_q$
vertices admits a bounded-error quantum algorithm that outputs a
monochromatic $K$-clique using
\[
 O\!\left(r^2\sqrt{L_q}\log(2r)\log\frac1\eta\right)
\]
colour-oracle queries in the worst case, where $r$, $B_r$, and $L_q$ are as
defined above.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Small-instance numerical experiments}
\label{qua:app:experiments}

\subparagraph*{Ideal-sampler recursion.}
We ran the scale-aware recursion at $K=3$, $N=16$, and $r=3$ for 1,000 trials
in each of five graph families.  The error schedule is
$(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)=(1/64,1/64,1/32)$, with sample
counts $m_i=\lceil\log(600)/(2\varepsilon_i^2)\rceil$; this assigns total
estimation-failure budget $0.01$.  Pivots are uniform, majority-estimation
samples are independent with replacement, and ties select colour~1.
Quantum search is replaced by ideal uniform sampling, so this tests the
combinatorial recursion, not coherent search failures or query costs.

The deterministic inputs are the complete graph, the empty graph, and the
balanced complete bipartite graph $K_{8,8}$.  For the random inputs, one
$G(16,1/2)$ graph is held fixed across all 1,000 trials, whereas the final
family draws a fresh $G(16,1/2)$ graph for each trial.  Every returned triple
is checked; exhaustion or a nonhomogeneous output counts as failure.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\hline
Graph family on 16 vertices & failed/trials & minimum final $|S_3|$\\
\hline
complete & $0/1000$ & 13\\
empty & $0/1000$ & 13\\
balanced complete bipartite $K_{8,8}$ & $0/1000$ & 6\\
one fixed $G(16,1/2)$ & $0/1000$ & 2\\
fresh $G(16,1/2)$ per trial & $0/1000$ & 2\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

All 5,000 trials returned homogeneous triples.  The table also reports the
smallest final candidate-set size observed within each family.  Zero observed
failures do not establish zero failure probability.

\subparagraph*{Isolated Grover sampler.}
We separately evolved a 16-dimensional state vector initialized to the
uniform superposition, with marked-set sizes $1,2,3,4,8,15$.  We averaged the
measurement distributions over a uniformly chosen number of Grover iterations
from zero through four.  The probability of measuring a marked item ranged
from $0.4026746749$ to $0.5973253251$.  Conditional on that outcome, the
largest deviation from the uniform distribution on marked items was zero
to machine precision.  This experiment illustrates the symmetry used in
\cref{qua:lem:capped-search}; it does not simulate its full capped search schedule.

\subparagraph*{Finite split-tree survival.}
Minimizing the ideal size-biased survival probability over every admissible
colour-class split gives exact finite-depth comparisons with our bounds.
For nine binary levels starting with 1,024 candidates, the minimum was
approximately $0.5086135566$, above the proved lower bound $513/1024$.
For four ternary levels starting with 128 candidates, it was approximately
$0.7155732457$, above $88/127$.  These are small-instance checks, not full
coherent simulations, hardware experiments, or speedup measurements.
